passages.happening:
“Now Jephthah the Gileadite was a mighty man of valor; he was the son of a prostitute, and Gilead was his father” (verse 1). His father's wife bears other sons, and when they grow up they drive Jephthah out. “You shall have no inheritance in our father’s house, because you are the son of another woman” (verse 2). He flees to the land of Tob, and worthless men gather around him (verse 3).

When the Ammonites make war on Israel, the elders of Gilead go to fetch him. “Come,” they said, “be our commander, so that we can fight against the Ammonites” (verse 6).

Jephthah answers, “Did you not hate me and expel me from my father’s house? Why then have you come to me now, when you are in distress?” (verse 7). They raise their offer: he will be leader over all Gilead. He makes them promise it, and they swear before the LORD (verses 8-10). The people make him their leader and commander, and Jephthah repeats all his terms before the LORD at Mizpah (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
Inheritance passed to a father's legitimate sons. A son born to a prostitute had no secure claim, and Jephthah's brothers used that against him. He became something the ancient world knew well: a man pushed out of his family, leading a band of other men with nowhere to belong, living by raiding or by hiring out to fight. Tob was a region to the north or northeast of Gilead.

Then his brothers' town needed him. The scene is full of old hurt. Jephthah does not let the elders forget what was done to him.

It is also a bargain. The elders first offer him the post of commander, a military chief for the war. When he presses them, they offer to make him head over all Gilead. He makes them swear to it before the LORD. Jephthah is a man who has learned to secure what he can before anyone can take it away. The chapter will show him bargaining three times: with the elders, with the king of Ammon, and with God.

Verse 1 calls him what the angel had called Gideon, ‘a mighty man of valor’. A man rejected by his family is the one God will use.
passages.later:
The pattern of a rejected brother who is needed later runs through the story of Joseph, sold by his brothers and later their rescuer (Genesis 45:4-7).

Men of Tob appear again as soldiers for hire, in the days of David: “twelve thousand men from Tob” (2 Samuel 10:6).
passages.asks: Jephthah's brothers threw him out, and then needed him. Ask whether you have shut anyone out who may one day be the person you need. And if you have been the one shut out, ask how that wound shapes the way you make your bargains with people, and with God.

passages.t: Jephthah's message to the king of Ammon
passages.happening:
Before fighting, Jephthah sends messengers to the king of the Ammonites and asks why he has come to fight (verse 12). The king answers that when Israel came out of Egypt it took his land, from the Arnon to the Jabbok, and he wants it back (verse 13).

Jephthah sends a long reply. Israel did not take the land of Moab or of Ammon (verse 15). When Israel came out of Egypt, it asked the kings of Edom and Moab for passage and was refused, so it went around them (verses 16-18). Then it asked Sihon, king of the Amorites, to let it pass. Sihon attacked instead, and the LORD gave his land to Israel (verses 19-22). “Do you not possess whatever your god Chemosh grants you? So also, we possess whatever the LORD our God has granted us” (verse 24). Israel has lived there three hundred years, he says. Why make the claim now? (verse 26).

“I have not sinned against you, but you have done me wrong by waging war against me. May the LORD, the Judge, decide today between the Israelites and the Ammonites” (verse 27). The king pays no attention (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
The quarrel was about the land between two rivers, the Arnon in the south and the Jabbok in the north, east of the Jordan. Jephthah's answer retells the history found in the books of Numbers and Deuteronomy. Israel had gone around Edom and Moab when they refused it passage. It took this land not from Ammon or Moab but from Sihon, an Amorite king who attacked Israel. Deuteronomy even records that Israel was told not to take Ammonite land at all, which supports his case.

He speaks in terms the king would accept. He talks of Chemosh as the god who gives the Ammonites their land. Chemosh was in fact the god of Moab; the god of Ammon was Milcom. Scholars explain this in different ways: the disputed land had once been Moab's, Ammon may have been speaking for Moab's claim, or the worship of the two peoples overlapped in that region.

The figure of three hundred years in verse 26 is often discussed in debates about the date of the exodus. Those who hold the earlier date, in the fifteenth century BC, see support for it here. Others read it as a round number, or as the sum of overlapping years, in a speech meant to persuade. The chapter does not settle the question.

The high point of the speech is verse 27. Jephthah calls on ‘the LORD, the Judge’. The book is named for this word. The true Judge is God, and the human judges are only his servants. Jephthah is right to put the case in God's hands. The tragedy is that he will not leave it there.
passages.later: The history Jephthah tells is in the book of Numbers: “Then Israel sent messengers to Sihon king of the Amorites” (Numbers 21:21), and Sihon refused and fought them at Jahaz. Moses had also been told, “I will not give you any of the land of the Ammonites. I have given it to the descendants of Lot as their possession” (Deuteronomy 2:19).
passages.asks: Jephthah argued his case carefully and then left it with ‘the LORD, the Judge’. Ask whether there is a dispute in your life that you need to put in God's hands, having said what is true. And ask whether you can leave it there, or whether you keep reaching to secure the outcome yourself.

passages.t: The Spirit, the vow, and the victory
passages.happening:
“Then the Spirit of the LORD came upon Jephthah” (verse 29). He passes through Gilead and Manasseh and advances against the Ammonites.

Then he makes a vow. “If indeed You will deliver the Ammonites into my hand, then whatever comes out the door of my house to greet me on my triumphant return from the Ammonites will belong to the LORD, and I will offer it up as a burnt offering” (verses 30-31).

He fights the Ammonites, and the LORD gives them into his hand. He strikes twenty towns, and the Ammonites are brought low before Israel (verses 32-33).
passages.hearers:
The order matters. The Spirit of the LORD comes on Jephthah first. Then he makes his vow. He did not need to bargain for God's help. God had already given it.

A vow was a solemn promise to God, usually with a condition: if God would do one thing, the one who vowed would do another. Jacob and Hannah both made vows, and Israel took vows seriously. But the law also gave ways for things and people vowed to God to be redeemed with money, and the law never allowed a vow to require what God forbids.

Jephthah's vow uses the ordinary word for a burnt offering, a sacrifice burned whole on the altar. Readers have long asked what he expected to come out of his house to meet him. The text does not say what he had in mind. It says what he promised.

Jephthah bargained with the elders, and he bargained with the king. Now he bargains with God, as if God's help had to be bought. That is the root of what follows.
passages.later:
The wisdom books warn against exactly this: “It is a trap for a man to dedicate something rashly, only later to reconsider his vows” (Proverbs 20:25), and “It is better not to vow than to make a vow and not fulfill it” (Ecclesiastes 5:5).

The law set out ways for vows involving people to be valued and redeemed: “When someone makes a special vow to the LORD involving the value of persons” (Leviticus 27:2).
passages.asks: The Spirit had already come on Jephthah, and still he made a deal. Ask where you try to bargain with God for something he has already given. And ask what promises you have made in a moment of fear that you should never have made, and whom you could ask for help with them.

passages.happening:
Jephthah comes home to Mizpah. “And when Jephthah returned home to Mizpah, there was his daughter coming out to meet him with tambourines and dancing! She was his only child; he had no son or daughter besides her” (verse 34).

When he sees her, he tears his clothes. “No! Not my daughter! You have brought me to my knees! You have brought great misery upon me, for I have given my word to the LORD and cannot take it back” (verse 35).

“My father,” she replied, “you have given your word to the LORD. Do to me as you have said, for the LORD has avenged you of your enemies, the Ammonites” (verse 36). She asks for two months to go into the hills with her friends and mourn that she will never marry. He lets her go (verses 37-38).

‘After two months, she returned to her father, and he did to her as he had vowed’ (verse 39). She had never known a man. From then on it becomes a custom that every year the young women of Israel go out for four days to lament the daughter of Jephthah (verses 39-40).
passages.hearers:
Women went out with tambourines and dancing to welcome men home from war, as Miriam did after the Red Sea and as the women later did for David. Jephthah's daughter does what a loving daughter would do. That is what makes the scene so terrible.

She is his only child. The Hebrew word is the one used of Isaac, ‘your only son’, in Genesis 22.

Listen to Jephthah's first words. They are spoken to her: ‘You have brought great misery upon me.’ They are words of grief, and they are about his own loss and his own vow.

She is never named. The yearly mourning of the young women of Israel is the only memorial she is given, and the book records it. She is remembered.

The narrator does not describe what was done. He says only that Jephthah did to her as he had vowed. The hard question below sets out how that sentence has been read.
passages.later:
The Bible's story of a father, an only child and an altar ends the other way in Genesis. The angel said to Abraham, “Do not lay a hand on the boy or do anything to him” (Genesis 22:12), and a ram was offered in Isaac's place.

The prophets speak of the sacrifice of children with horror, in God's own words: “something I never commanded, nor did it even enter My mind” (Jeremiah 7:31). And Micah answers the question of whether God wants a firstborn offered: “He has shown you, O man, what is good. And what does the LORD require of you but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?” (Micah 6:8).
passages.hard:
Did Jephthah really put his daughter to death? And why does the text not condemn him?

Most readers, Jewish and Christian, ancient and modern, have understood the chapter to describe a real human sacrifice. The vow uses the word for a burnt offering, and verse 39 says that he did to her as he had vowed. On this reading the narrator's silence is not approval. Judges often reports terrible acts without comment and lets the law supply the verdict. The chapter stands in a book about Israel's moral collapse, and the daughter is mourned every year. Everything points to tragedy, not to faithfulness.

A smaller number of readers, among them some medieval Jewish interpreters and some Christian readers since, hold that Jephthah gave his daughter to lifelong service at the sanctuary, unmarried. They point out that she mourns her virginity and not her death, that verse 39 adds that she had never known a man, and that the small word joining the two halves of verse 31 can also be read as or. Those who disagree answer that nothing else in the Old Testament describes such a vow of lifelong service for women, and that the plain sense of burnt offering is hard to avoid.

These notes set out both readings and do not choose between them. But some things must be said plainly on either reading. Nothing in this chapter praises the vow. Scripture elsewhere forbids the sacrifice of children as an abomination: “You must not worship the LORD your God in this way, because they practice for their gods every abomination which the LORD hates. They even burn their sons and daughters in the fire as sacrifices to their gods” (Deuteronomy 12:31). Hebrews names Jephthah among those who acted by faith (Hebrews 11:32), which shows that God worked through him despite the vow, not that the vow was right. And no one today is ever asked by God to harm a child.

A word for anyone who was not protected by a parent, or was handed over to harm by someone who should have kept them safe. This story does not call that right. What was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. If you are still in danger, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The young women of Israel remembered Jephthah's daughter every year, though no one recorded her name. Ask whom you could remember who suffered for someone else's foolish promise or pride. And ask whether there is a promise you have made, to God or to anyone, that is harming someone else, and who could help you be released from it.
